title: Rate limiter
scopeHtml: Scope: Token bucket, sliding window log and counter, pluggable strategies, per-key concurrency.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design a rate limiter that decides, for each request key (user id, IP, API key), whether to allow or reject it, with the algorithm pluggable: token bucket, sliding window log, sliding window counter.

Clarify: limit per what (user, IP, endpoint)? What numbers (for example 100 requests per minute)? Is burst allowed? Single machine or distributed? Reject with HTTP 429 plus Retry-After? Fail open or closed if the limiter breaks? (Here: in-process, per-key, one interface, three strategies.)

Worked example. Limit 5 requests/s with burst 5: a client sends 10 at once; 5 pass, 5 get 429; two seconds later 2 more tokens exist if refill is 1/s. At a gateway taking 50,000 requests/s, a single abusive client sending 5,000/s would eat 10% of capacity without a limiter.

Industry examples. Stripe (token bucket on requests, plus concurrency limiters), GitHub API (5,000 requests/hour per token with X-RateLimit-* headers), Cloudflare, NGINX limit_req (leaky bucket), AWS API Gateway (token bucket), Envoy and Kong global rate-limit services backed by Redis.

Everyday analogy. A bouncer who lets in at most N people per minute, and the queue outside keeps its own count per group.

Common interview traps.

  • Not asking per-what. A global limit is a different design from per-user.
  • Forgetting the response contract: 429 and Retry-After.
  • Skipping the fail-open vs fail-closed discussion.

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
• RateLimiter (interface): allow(): boolean. One instance guards one key.
  • TokenBucket, SlidingWindowLog, SlidingWindowCounter: strategies.
  • RateLimiterService: map from key to limiter, created on first use through a factory.
  • Clock (LongSupplier): injected for testability.

Design choice: each limiter object holds the state for one key, and the service owns the key map. That keeps the algorithms tiny (no key handling) and makes the lock per key.

Decision gravity. The allow() interface is the one-way door; algorithms behind it can be changed per route or per customer tier without touching callers. Per-key state in memory is reversible to a Redis-backed version by swapping the factory.

Everyday analogy. Every customer has their own punch card; the shop only needs to look at that card, not at everyone's.

Common interview traps.

  • A single global counter shared by all users.
  • Algorithms that need a timer thread per key (millions of keys). Prefer lazy computation on each call.

notes.title: Class diagram
notes.html:
<<interface>>
   +--------------------+
   | RateLimiter        |
   | allow(): boolean   |
   +--------------------+
     ^        ^         ^
+-----------+ +------------------+ +----------------------+
|TokenBucket| |SlidingWindowLog  | |SlidingWindowCounter  |
| capacity  | | limit,windowMs   | | limit,windowMs       |
| refill/ms | | stamps: Deque    | | cur, prev, curStart  |
| tokens    | +------------------+ +----------------------+
| last      |
+-----------+

+--------------------------------------+
| RateLimiterService                   |
| byKey: ConcurrentHashMap<key,Limiter>|
| factory: Supplier<RateLimiter>       |
| allow(key): boolean                  |
+--------------------------------------+

How to read it. The service holds the factory, so the same service class can be used with any strategy by passing () -> new TokenBucket(...).

Common interview traps.

  • Passing the clock as a static System.currentTimeMillis(); tests then need sleep.
  • Mixing the key map into each algorithm.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• Strategy (RateLimiter): algorithms are interchangeable. Why: different endpoints want different behaviour (login: strict; search: burst friendly). Alternative: one class with a mode enum (grows branches). Reversible.
  • Factory (Supplier<RateLimiter>): the service creates a limiter per key, without knowing the concrete type.
  • Lazy refill: compute the new token count from elapsed time on each call; no background timer. O(1) per call, O(1) memory per key.

Comparison (the table interviewers love):

Algorithm Memory per key Accuracy Allows bursts Notes
Fixed window counter 1 counter Poor at window edges (2x burst across a boundary) Yes, at edges Simplest; Redis INCR + EXPIRE
Sliding window log one timestamp per request (up to the limit) Exact No Memory heavy for large limits
Sliding window counter 2 counters Approximate (assumes even spread in the previous window) Mild Cloudflare reported this to be very accurate in practice
Token bucket 2 numbers (tokens, last time) Exact for its model Yes, up to capacity Common default (Stripe, AWS)
Leaky bucket a queue or counter Smooths output rate No NGINX limit_req

Worked example (sliding window counter). Limit 10 per 1,000 ms. Previous window had 10 requests, current window is 50% elapsed, current count 0. Estimate = 10 x 0.5 + 0 = 5, so 5 more are allowed, matching the test.

Everyday analogy. Token bucket: a jar that gains a coin every second (max 5) and each visit spends one. Sliding log: a notebook listing exact visit times from the last minute.

Common interview traps.

  • Fixed window edge case: 100 requests at 12:00:59 and 100 at 12:01:00 are both "allowed" but that is 200 in two seconds.
  • Claiming sliding window counter is exact. It is an estimate.

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
Full runnable file Main.java (three strategies, per-key service, tests including a concurrent one):

import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import java.util.function.*;

/** Strategy interface: one instance guards ONE key (user, IP, API key). */
interface RateLimiter {
    boolean allow();
}

/** Token bucket: allows bursts up to capacity, long-run rate = refillPerSec. Lazy refill, no timer thread. */
class TokenBucket implements RateLimiter {
    private final double capacity, refillPerMs; private final LongSupplier clock;
    private double tokens; private long last;
    TokenBucket(int capacity, double refillPerSec, LongSupplier clock) {
        this.capacity = capacity; this.refillPerMs = refillPerSec / 1000.0; this.clock = clock;
        this.tokens = capacity; this.last = clock.getAsLong();
    }
    public synchronized boolean allow() {
        long now = clock.getAsLong();
        tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - last) * refillPerMs);
        last = now;
        if (tokens >= 1) { tokens -= 1; return true; }
        return false;
    }
}

/** Sliding window log: exact, but stores one timestamp per accepted request (memory = limit). */
class SlidingWindowLog implements RateLimiter {
    private final int limit; private final long windowMs; private final LongSupplier clock;
    private final ArrayDeque<Long> stamps = new ArrayDeque<>();
    SlidingWindowLog(int limit, long windowMs, LongSupplier clock) { this.limit = limit; this.windowMs = windowMs; this.clock = clock; }
    public synchronized boolean allow() {
        long now = clock.getAsLong();
        while (!stamps.isEmpty() && stamps.peekFirst() <= now - windowMs) stamps.pollFirst();
        if (stamps.size() >= limit) return false;
        stamps.addLast(now);
        return true;
    }
}

/** Sliding window counter: two counters, weighted estimate. O(1) memory, small approximation error. */
class SlidingWindowCounter implements RateLimiter {
    private final int limit; private final long windowMs; private final LongSupplier clock;
    private long curStart; private int cur, prev;
    SlidingWindowCounter(int limit, long windowMs, LongSupplier clock) {
        this.limit = limit; this.windowMs = windowMs; this.clock = clock; this.curStart = clock.getAsLong();
    }
    public synchronized boolean allow() {
        long now = clock.getAsLong();
        long elapsedWindows = (now - curStart) / windowMs;
        if (elapsedWindows >= 1) {                       // roll the window forward
            prev = elapsedWindows == 1 ? cur : 0;
            cur = 0; curStart += elapsedWindows * windowMs;
        }
        double fractionOfPrev = 1.0 - (double) (now - curStart) / windowMs;
        if (prev * fractionOfPrev + cur >= limit) return false;
        cur++;
        return true;
    }
}

/** Per-key registry. computeIfAbsent is atomic so two threads never create two buckets for one key. */
class RateLimiterService {
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, RateLimiter> byKey = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Supplier<RateLimiter> factory;
    RateLimiterService(Supplier<RateLimiter> factory) { this.factory = factory; }
    boolean allow(String key) { return byKey.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> factory.get()).allow(); }
}

public class Main {
    static void check(boolean c, String msg) { if (!c) throw new AssertionError(msg); }
    static int run(RateLimiter rl, int n) { int ok = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (rl.allow()) ok++; return ok; }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        long[] t = {0}; LongSupplier clock = () -> t[0];

        RateLimiter tb = new TokenBucket(5, 1.0, clock);              // burst 5, then 1/sec
        check(run(tb, 10) == 5, "burst of 5");
        t[0] += 2000;
        check(run(tb, 10) == 2, "2 tokens refilled after 2s");

        t[0] = 0; RateLimiter log = new SlidingWindowLog(3, 1000, clock);
        check(run(log, 5) == 3, "3 per window");
        t[0] = 999; check(!log.allow(), "still inside window");
        t[0] = 1000; check(log.allow(), "oldest aged out");

        t[0] = 0; RateLimiter swc = new SlidingWindowCounter(10, 1000, clock);
        check(run(swc, 10) == 10, "fills window");
        t[0] = 1500;                                                  // half of previous window still counts: 10*0.5=5
        check(run(swc, 10) == 5, "weighted estimate allows 5 more");

        // pluggable + concurrent: 1 key, 200 threads-worth of calls, capacity 50, no refill => exactly 50 pass
        RateLimiterService svc = new RateLimiterService(() -> new TokenBucket(50, 0, () -> 0L));
        AtomicInteger allowed = new AtomicInteger();
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);
        for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) pool.submit(() -> { if (svc.allow("user-1")) allowed.incrementAndGet(); });
        pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        check(allowed.get() == 50, "exactly 50, got " + allowed.get());
        check(svc.allow("user-2"), "other keys are independent");
        System.out.println("P11 OK");
    }
}

The core in Kotlin:

fun interface RateLimiter { fun allow(): Boolean }

class TokenBucket(private val capacity: Int, refillPerSec: Double,
                  private val clock: () -> Long) : RateLimiter {
    private val refillPerMs = refillPerSec / 1000.0
    private var tokens = capacity.toDouble()
    private var last = clock()

    @Synchronized override fun allow(): Boolean {
        val now = clock()
        tokens = minOf(capacity.toDouble(), tokens + (now - last) * refillPerMs)
        last = now
        return if (tokens >= 1) { tokens -= 1; true } else false
    }
}

class SlidingWindowLog(private val limit: Int, private val windowMs: Long,
                       private val clock: () -> Long) : RateLimiter {
    private val stamps = ArrayDeque<Long>()
    @Synchronized override fun allow(): Boolean {
        val now = clock()
        while (stamps.isNotEmpty() && stamps.first() <= now - windowMs) stamps.removeFirst()
        if (stamps.size >= limit) return false
        stamps.addLast(now); return true
    }
}

class RateLimiterService(private val factory: () -> RateLimiter) {
    private val byKey = java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<String, RateLimiter>()
    fun allow(key: String) = byKey.computeIfAbsent(key) { factory() }.allow()
}

Walk-through (token bucket). Capacity 5, refill 1/s, clock 0: 5 calls pass (tokens 0). Call 6 fails. Clock jumps to 2,000 ms: tokens = min(5, 0 + 2000 x 0.001) = 2, so exactly 2 more pass.

Common interview traps.

  • Not capping tokens at capacity after a long idle (an hour of idle gives 3,600 tokens).
  • int math on time deltas overflowing; use long.
  • Using <= vs < at window boundaries inconsistently.

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
javac Main.java && java -ea Main
# prints: P11 OK

The test drives a fake clock. Token bucket: burst of 5 passes, 2 more after 2 s. Sliding log: 3 per window, rejected at 999 ms, allowed at 1,000 ms when the oldest ages out. Sliding counter: weighted estimate lets exactly 5 through. Concurrency: 200 tasks on 8 threads hit one key whose bucket has capacity 50 and no refill; exactly 50 pass. A second key is unaffected.

Common interview traps.

  • Tests that rely on Thread.sleep; they are slow and flaky.
  • No test for two keys being independent.

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
Two layers of shared state:

  1. Inside one limiter: the read-modify-write of tokens is not atomic. Two threads could both read tokens = 1, both decrement, and both be allowed. Fix: synchronized on the limiter (per key, so different keys do not contend), or a CAS loop on an AtomicLong that packs tokens and timestamp. The test proves exactly 50 of 200 pass.
  2. The key map: ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent is atomic per key, so two threads never create two limiters for one key (which would double the allowance). Keep the factory cheap; it runs inside the map's bin lock.

Going distributed. In-process limits multiply by the number of servers (10 servers each allowing 100/min gives 1,000/min). Options:

  • Central Redis with a Lua script (atomic): GET tokens, last; compute; SET with EXPIRE. One round trip of about 0.5 ms; at 100k keys/s one Redis handles it, shard by key hash beyond that. Stripe and many API gateways do this.
  • Local token slice + periodic sync: each node takes tokens from the central store in chunks of 10; cheaper, slightly over-admits.
  • Sticky routing: send a key's traffic to the same node (consistent hashing) and keep local state; fast but fails over poorly.

Fail open or closed? If Redis is down, rejecting all traffic is an outage caused by the limiter. Most public APIs fail open (allow) with an alert; login or payment endpoints may fail closed.

Memory: idle keys leak. Evict limiters not touched for a window (Caffeine cache with expireAfterAccess) or use Redis TTLs: 10M keys x about 100 bytes = about 1 GB.

Incident pattern. Clock skew between nodes with a timestamp-based limiter in Redis causes early or late resets; use the Redis server time (TIME in Lua), not client time.

Decision gravity. Choosing fail-open vs fail-closed is a business decision per endpoint; make it configurable from day one (easy to change later, painful to discover during an outage).

Everyday analogy. Several ticket counters sharing one sign saying how many tickets are left; if each had its own sign, you could sell the same last ticket at every counter.

Common interview traps.

  • Check-then-set in Redis with separate GET and SET (race); use Lua or INCR.
  • Using wall clock in tests and in production without a monotonic source for elapsed time (JVM: System.nanoTime is monotonic; wall-clock can jump).

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• Tiered limits: free vs paid plans, via a limiter factory chosen by plan.
  • Multiple rules per request: per second AND per day; allow only if all pass (compose limiters).
  • Response headers: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, Retry-After; then allow() should return a result object with remaining and reset time.
  • Weighted requests: expensive endpoints cost more tokens (tryAcquire(n)).
  • Concurrency limiter: cap in-flight requests rather than rate (a semaphore).
  • Dynamic config: hot-reload limits without a deploy.
  • Load shedding vs rate limiting: shedding protects the server by priority under overload; limiting enforces fairness per client.

Common interview traps.

  • Returning only a boolean when the API needs Retry-After.
  • Limiting by IP only (NAT puts thousands of users behind one IP); combine with user or API key.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• One RateLimiter interface per key; strategies: token bucket (bursty, default), sliding log (exact, memory heavy), sliding counter (2 numbers, approximate), fixed window (edge-burst flaw).
  • Refill lazily from elapsed time; inject the clock; cap tokens at capacity.
  • Per-key synchronized plus ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent makes it thread-safe; the test proves exactly N of M requests pass.
  • Distributed: Redis plus Lua for atomicity, TTLs for cleanup, decide fail-open or fail-closed.
  • Always mention 429 and Retry-After, and what the key is.

questions.promptHtml: Why do most API gateways use a token bucket instead of a simple fixed-window counter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks that you know the edge-burst flaw of the simplest algorithm and can state what each algorithm trades.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A fixed window counts requests per clock minute, so a client can send 100 at 12:00:59 and 100 at 12:01:00: 200 requests in two seconds while "within the limit". A token bucket stores two numbers, tokens and last-refill time, refills lazily from elapsed time, and caps at capacity. It allows a controlled burst, enforces the long-run rate, and costs O(1) memory per key with no timer thread.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Fixed window: one counter per key per window. Simple (Redis INCR + EXPIRE), but up to 2x the limit can pass across a window boundary.
  • Token bucket: tokens = min(capacity, tokens + elapsed * refillRate); a request needs 1 token. Capacity is the burst, refill rate is the sustained rate.
  • Sliding log is exact but stores one timestamp per accepted request; sliding counter stores 2 counters and estimates.
Fixed window, limit 100/min:
 12:00:59 -> 100 allowed   | boundary |  12:01:00 -> 100 allowed
 => 200 requests in 2 seconds
Token bucket (cap 100, 100/min): the second burst finds ~0 tokens and is rejected.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Not capping tokens at capacity: an hour idle gives 3,600 tokens.
  • Claiming sliding window counter is exact; it assumes an even spread in the previous window.
  • Using a background timer to refill millions of keys.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you allow bursts but not sustained overload? -> Token bucket: capacity is burst size, refill rate is the sustained limit.
  2. When would you pick sliding log anyway? -> Small limits (for example 5 login attempts per minute) where exactness matters and memory equals the limit.
  3. Why leaky bucket in NGINX limit_req? -> It smooths output to a constant rate (queue), which protects a backend that cannot take bursts.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "token bucket allows bursts". The senior answer quantifies the fixed-window 2x flaw, names memory per key for each algorithm, and ties the choice to the endpoint (login strict, search burst-friendly).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team capped an export API with fixed windows; a client's scheduler fired at :59 and :00 and doubled the load on the database every minute.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate sends this token bucket for review. In a load test with capacity 50 and no refill, 200 calls from 8 threads let 63 through. After one night idle, a client got a burst of thousands.

class TokenBucket implements RateLimiter {
    private double tokens, capacity, refillPerMs; private long last; private final LongSupplier clock;
    TokenBucket(int cap, double perSec, LongSupplier clock) {
        capacity = cap; refillPerMs = perSec / 1000; this.clock = clock; tokens = cap; last = clock.getAsLong();
    }
    public boolean allow() {
        long now = clock.getAsLong();
        tokens = tokens + (now - last) * refillPerMs;
        last = now;
        if (tokens >= 1) { tokens -= 1; return true; }
        return false;
    }
}
class TokenBucket(private val capacity: Double, perSec: Double, private val clock: () -> Long) : RateLimiter {
    private val refillPerMs = perSec / 1000
    private var tokens = capacity
    private var last = clock()
    override fun allow(): Boolean {
        val now = clock()
        tokens += (now - last) * refillPerMs
        last = now
        return if (tokens >= 1) { tokens -= 1; true } else false
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find every bug and fix it. How would you prove the fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Notices only "not thread safe" and wraps the whole service in one global synchronized, which makes all keys contend. Misses the missing cap entirely.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is one instance per key (yes, per the design)? Does the limit need to be exact or approximate under contention? Is the clock injectable and monotonic?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident, but the burst-after-idle bug is a live over-admission; I would ship the cap first because it is a one-line fix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) No min(capacity, ...): tokens grow unbounded while idle, so an idle client gets a huge burst. (b) allow() is a read-modify-write on tokens and last; two threads read tokens = 1, both decrement, both get true, which explains 63 > 50. (c) Smaller: (now - last) is a long and fine, but wall-clock jumps backwards would give negative refill; use a monotonic source.
  4. How I'd verify each: Fake clock: call allow() after t += 3_600_000 and assert only capacity calls pass. For the race: 200 tasks on 8 threads at capacity 50 with refill 0, assert exactly 50.
  5. Root cause: Unbounded refill plus unsynchronized compound state update.
  6. Fix: tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + elapsed * refillPerMs) and mark allow() synchronized (per key, so different keys never contend). Longer term, a CAS loop on an AtomicLong packing tokens and timestamp if the lock shows up in a profile.
  7. Prevention: Keep the concurrent test (exactly N of M) and the idle-hour test in CI; reject Date/currentTimeMillis in limiters by injecting the clock.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use one global lock (all users serialize) and would not add a timer thread per key (millions of threads).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Lock contention shows up for one hot key at 50k req/s? -> Shard that key's bucket into N sub-buckets with capacity/N each (slightly less accurate) or use the CAS version.
  • System clock steps back 5 s? -> Use System.nanoTime for elapsed time and clamp negative deltas to 0.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of an incident where an unsynchronized bucket "mostly worked" in staging and over-admitted by 30% in production only during peak, which is exactly when the limiter mattered.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only says "add synchronized to the service".
  • Hire: finds the race and the missing cap, fixes both, writes the concurrent test.
  • Strong hire: also discusses per-key lock scope, monotonic time, CAS alternative and hot-key sharding.

questions.contextHtml: Your in-process limiter returns a boolean. Product now says: free plan gets 10 requests/second and 1,000/day, paid gets 100/second and 50,000/day. The mobile team also needs X-RateLimit-Remaining and Retry-After on every 429. About 40 call sites use limiter.allow(key).
questions.promptHtml: Which classes change, which do not, and how do you keep the call sites stable?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds if (plan == FREE) branches inside the token bucket and returns a string. The algorithm now knows about plans and every caller breaks.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must all rules pass (AND)? Does a rejected request consume tokens in the other limiter? Is the daily window calendar-based or rolling? Who decides the plan (auth layer)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable; plan the change so old callers still compile.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Options: (a) change allow() to return a result object; (b) add tryAcquire() returning a result and keep allow() as a thin wrapper; (c) put headers in a separate method. I pick (b): reversible and call sites migrate gradually.
  4. How I'd verify: Unit tests with a fake clock: free plan passes 10 in one second, 11th rejected with retryAfterMs equal to the time until the next token; daily rule rejects the 1,001st request even when the per-second rule would pass.
  5. Root cause / design: A CompositeLimiter implements RateLimiter holding a list of limiters; it allows only if all allow. The factory in RateLimiterService is chosen by plan (Function<Plan, Supplier<RateLimiter>>). Result object: allowed, remaining, retryAfterMs.
  6. Fix (code):

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
record Decision(boolean allowed, long remaining, long retryAfterMs) {}

class CompositeLimiter implements RateLimiter {
    private final List<RateLimiter> all;
    CompositeLimiter(List<RateLimiter> all) { this.all = all; }
    public boolean allow() { return decide().allowed(); }
    Decision decide() {
        for (RateLimiter r : all) if (!r.allow()) return new Decision(false, 0, 1000);
        return new Decision(true, -1, 0);   // remaining: needs each limiter to expose it
    }
}
data class Decision(val allowed: Boolean, val remaining: Long, val retryAfterMs: Long)

class CompositeLimiter(private val all: List<RateLimiter>) : RateLimiter {
    override fun allow() = decide().allowed
    fun decide(): Decision {
        for (r in all) if (!r.allow()) return Decision(false, 0, 1000)
        return Decision(true, -1, 0)
    }
}
  1. Prevention: A note about the flaw above: when limiter 1 passes and limiter 2 rejects, limiter 1 already spent a token. To be exact, check both with a non-consuming peek first, then consume under one lock. Contract test per plan.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not hardcode plan names in algorithms; I would not return only a boolean when the API contract needs Retry-After.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Expensive endpoints should cost 5 tokens? -> tryAcquire(n); the bucket checks tokens >= n.
  • Plans change mid-session? -> Replace the limiter in the map (state resets) or resize capacity in place; decide and document.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of a billing-tier launch where the daily limiter was consumed by requests the per-second limiter had already rejected, so paying users hit their daily cap early.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds plan branches in the algorithm.
  • Hire: composite plus factory by plan, result object, stable call sites.
  • Strong hire: spots the consume-on-partial-failure flaw and proposes peek-then-commit.

questions.contextHtml: A public API has 5 million active API keys in a day. Proposal A: sliding window log, limit 1,000 requests per minute per key. Proposal B: sliding window counter. Typical key sends 30 requests/minute but the top 1% hit the limit. Another engineer says "log is exact so we must use it". The service has 16 GB of heap for limiter state.
questions.promptHtml: Compute memory for both and choose. State what accuracy you give up.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Exact is always better" without computing; or picks counter without knowing it is an estimate.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is a small over-admission (a few percent) acceptable? Is the limit a fairness tool or a billing contract? What happens at the boundary: is exactness contractual?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; decision under constraint.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Log memory per key is up to limit timestamps. Counter memory is 2 counters plus a window start.
  4. How I'd verify (the math): Log worst case, 50,000 hot keys (1%) x 1,000 stamps x 8 bytes boxed Long objects (about 16 to 24 bytes each with deque overhead, say 32) = about 1.6 GB; the typical 4.95M keys x 30 stamps x 32 bytes = about 4.75 GB. Total about 6.4 GB, tight with a 16 GB heap shared with the app and GC headroom. Counter: 5M keys x (2 ints + 1 long + object header, say 48 bytes) = about 240 MB.
  5. Root cause: Log memory scales with request volume, counter scales with key count.
  6. Fix / decision: Sliding window counter for the general API: roughly 25x less memory and O(1) per call. Worked estimate: previous window 10 requests, current window 50% elapsed, current count 0, limit 10: estimate 5, so 5 more pass. Keep a sliding log only for tiny strict limits like login (5/min).
  7. Prevention: Test with a replay of production traffic to measure the error versus a log reference; alert on p99 allowed-rate above limit by more than 5%.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I accept a small approximation, the sliding counter assumes even spread in the previous window; I would not use fixed window (2x boundary burst) and would not claim the counter is exact.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Billing depends on the limit being exact? -> Use the log for billed keys only, or count exactly (an AtomicLong per key per window) and treat rate limiting separately from metering.
  • Memory still grows with cardinality? -> Evict idle keys (Caffeine expireAfterAccess = window).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of a gateway that stored a timestamp per request and was killed by GC pauses as the heap filled with boxed Longs; switching to two counters dropped heap by an order of magnitude.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: no numbers.
  • Hire: computes both, picks the counter, names the approximation.
  • Strong hire: includes boxed overhead, hot-key skew, eviction and a measured-error plan.

questions.contextHtml:
You scaled from 1 to 10 app servers behind a load balancer and moved the counter to Redis. A limit of 100/min per user now lets about 130 through, and on one new server, users get reset early. The Redis code:

count = redis.GET("rl:user42")
if count == null: count = 0
if count < 100:
    redis.SET("rl:user42", count + 1, EX=60)   // client: now = System.currentTimeMillis()
    allow
else: reject

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Redis is single threaded so it is atomic": true per command, not across a GET then a SET. Misses the TTL reset and the clock skew.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are all servers using the same Redis key? Fixed or sliding window? What does Redis HA look like (replica reads)? Are server clocks synced (NTP)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: If over-admission is hurting the backend, lower the limit temporarily (for example 80) while fixing.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) GET then SET is check-then-act across a network: two servers read 99, both write 100 and both allow. (b) SET ... EX 60 on every request resets the TTL, so the "window" slides forever for active users, or if time is computed client-side, skewed clocks shift window boundaries. (c) Replica reads showing stale counts.
  4. How I'd verify: Fire 200 parallel requests from 10 clients with a script and count allowed; redis-cli MONITOR to watch interleaved GET/SET; compare date on servers.
  5. Root cause: Non-atomic read-modify-write over the network plus client time.
  6. Fix: One atomic operation. Fixed window: INCR key, and EXPIRE only when the result is 1. Token bucket: a Lua script that reads the key, uses Redis TIME (not client time), refills, decrements and sets TTL in one go. One round trip, about 0.5 ms.
  7. Prevention: A concurrency test against a real Redis in CI (testcontainers); never compute time on clients for shared state.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use a distributed lock around each request (extra latency, failure modes); local token slices with periodic sync are cheaper but slightly over-admit.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Redis latency becomes your p99? -> Local slice of tokens (take 10 at a time) and accept small over-admission.
  • Cluster resharding moves the key? -> The counter resets for that key; acceptable for rate limiting, not for billing.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of a limiter that passed all unit tests single-node and leaked 30% once the fleet grew, because limits multiplied by node count until the check moved into Redis.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames Redis.
  • Hire: identifies check-then-act and prescribes INCR or Lua.
  • Strong hire: also fixes time source, TTL handling, round-trip cost and the slice trade-off.

questions.contextHtml: The in-process limiter keeps a ConcurrentHashMap<String, RateLimiter> keyed by client IP. After a credential-stuffing attack from a botnet rotating IPs, the service restarts every 40 minutes with OOM. Heap histogram shows 38M TokenBucket objects, about 80 bytes each plus map entries. Normal traffic is 200k distinct IPs per day. The limiter code is unchanged for a year.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more heap" or "block the botnet in the firewall" only, leaving the unbounded map.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the key purely IP? Do idle limiters ever get removed? What is the heap size and GC pattern? Do we have a WAF in front?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart with a larger heap as a stopgap; at the edge, cap new-key creation rate or serve a global limit for never-seen keys; enable WAF rules for the attack.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The map never evicts, so every unique IP is a permanent entry. (b) A leak elsewhere (check the histogram, but 38M buckets is the evidence). (c) Large keys (full user-agent strings) inflate memory: red herring if keys are short.
  4. How I'd verify: jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram, a heap dump in Eclipse MAT, and a metric of map size over time.
  5. Root cause: Per-key state with no eviction, so an attacker controls memory by choosing keys. 38M x (80 + about 50 map overhead) is about 5 GB.
  6. Fix: Short-term: evict idle keys. Long-term: Caffeine cache with expireAfterAccess(window) and a maximum size; an evicted idle key resets to a full bucket, which is correct because it was idle anyway. Add a secondary global limit for unknown keys. Also move to Redis with TTL if state must be shared.
  7. Prevention: Gauge limiter.keys, alert on growth rate; a load test with random keys; a rule that any map keyed by external input must be bounded.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: With a max size, an attacker can evict a legitimate heavy user's state (they get a fresh bucket); acceptable, but I would note it. I would not use a timer thread per key.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Attacker evicts legitimate keys by flooding? -> Tiered: admit-by-recency (Caffeine W-TinyLFU favors frequent keys).
  • Key by IP hurts offices behind NAT? -> Combine with user or API key.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident where the limiter protecting login became the cause of an outage because its own state was attacker-controlled.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases the heap.
  • Hire: finds unbounded map, adds expiring cache.
  • Strong hire: addresses eviction side effects, NAT keys, edge mitigation and monitoring.

questions.promptHtml: How do you test a rate limiter whose behaviour depends on time without Thread.sleep?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Time-dependent code is the most common source of flaky tests; the answer shows design for testability.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I inject the clock as a LongSupplier (or Clock), so tests use a fake clock they advance by hand. The test is instant and deterministic: burst of 5 passes, advance 2,000 ms, exactly 2 more pass. I also test boundaries at 999 ms vs 1,000 ms, two keys being independent, and a concurrent test asserting counts, never ordering.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Production uses a monotonic source for elapsed time (System.nanoTime) because wall-clock can jump; tests substitute a long[] t captured by a lambda.
  • Boundary tests are where bugs hide: < vs <= at the window edge.
  • Concurrency test: 200 tasks on 8 threads on one key with capacity 50 and zero refill must yield exactly 50; refill 0 removes time from the assertion.
fake clock: t=0   -> 10 calls: 5 ok
            t=2000-> 10 calls: 2 ok   (2 tokens refilled)
sliding log (3 per 1000ms): t=999 rejected, t=1000 allowed

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
long[] t = {0};
RateLimiter tb = new TokenBucket(5, 1.0, () -> t[0]);
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) assert tb.allow();
assert !tb.allow();
t[0] += 2000;
assert tb.allow() && tb.allow() && !tb.allow();
var t = 0L
val tb = TokenBucket(5, 1.0) { t }
repeat(5) { check(tb.allow()) }
check(!tb.allow())
t += 2000
check(tb.allow() && tb.allow() && !tb.allow())

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Tests with Thread.sleep(1000): slow and flaky on loaded CI.
  • Asserting the order of results across threads.
  • No test that two keys do not share state.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you test the Redis version? -> Testcontainers with real Redis, plus a fake time source passed into the Lua args if you control it, otherwise accept Redis TIME.
  2. How do you test clock going backwards? -> Fake clock decreases; assert no negative refill and no exception.
  3. How do you test thread safety honestly? -> Many runs of the exact-count test; a stress run with jcstress-style tooling is the stronger check (verify it fits your build).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "mock time". Senior: design the seam (injected clock), pick boundary cases deliberately, and use count-based concurrent assertions with refill disabled.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A limiter shipped with a <= window bug that no test covered; it blocked every request exactly at the boundary millisecond and showed up as periodic 429 spikes.

questions.contextHtml: Rate limiting runs as a Redis-backed check in the gateway for all routes: public search (60k req/s), login (800 req/s) and payments (300 req/s). At 02:10 Redis primary fails over; for 45 seconds each limiter call times out after 200 ms. Gateway p99 climbs from 40 ms to 2.4 s, threads saturate, and error rate hits 70% on everything. Your manager says: "Just make the limiter fail closed so we are safe from abuse."
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong, what do you change, and how do you answer your manager?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks a single policy for every route ("fail open everywhere" or "closed everywhere") and ignores that the 200 ms timeout itself caused the outage.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the per-route business risk of over-admission versus rejection? Is there a local fallback state? What is the abuse we fear on login (credential stuffing) versus search?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Trip a circuit breaker on the limiter dependency: skip the Redis call after 50 ms or after N consecutive failures, and fall back to a local in-process limit (per-node limit = global limit / nodes).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The limiter is on the critical path with a long timeout, so a slow dependency exhausts threads (the real cause). (b) Fail-closed turned a Redis blip into total outage. (c) Failover itself was slow: red herring for this design question.
  4. How I'd verify: Thread dump showing threads parked in the Redis client; timeline of limiter latency vs gateway latency; connection pool metrics.
  5. Root cause: A synchronous dependency with a timeout longer than the budget, and no degraded mode.
  6. Fix: Short timeout (10 to 20 ms) plus breaker. Policy per route, configurable from day one: search fails open with a local limiter fallback and an alert; login fails closed on a local strict limiter (not "reject everything", just a conservative cap); payments fail closed. Decision gravity: policy is a business decision and easy to change, but discovering it during an outage is the costly path.
  7. Prevention: Chaos test killing Redis monthly; alert on limiter fallback rate; dashboards of limiter latency in the p99 budget.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not blindly fail closed (limiter becomes the outage) and would not fail fully open on login (an attacker waits for failovers).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Local fallback over-admits by node count? -> Divide the limit by node count; accept 2x error for 45 seconds.
  • Redis client time vs server time during failover? -> Use Redis TIME; a promoted replica may have a different clock.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident where a "protection" layer's timeout config was the single longest in the request path, so it caused more downtime than the attacks it blocked.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: agrees with the manager or picks one global policy.
  • Hire: per-route policy, short timeout and breaker.
  • Strong hire: local fallback math, chaos testing, and framing it as a business decision with a one-way-door risk if discovered late.
